title: Electric bill shock! How to avoid 'emergency heat' costs
summary: TV consumer report on neighbourhood electric bill shocks, traced to a longer billing cycle, cold weather and faulty heat pumps running on emergency heat.

assertions.quote: THE AUXILIARY POWER OR EMERGENCY HEAT KICKS IN AND THAT SUCKS THREE TIMES THE ENERGY.
IF THE HEAT PUMP FAILS IN THAT SAME UNIT, YOU WON'T KNOW IT BECAUSE OF THE AUXILIARY POWER.

verdicts.note: Backup strips keep the house warm when the compressor fails, so the fault often shows up only as a high bill.

At Site 2 a control or sensor fault left the compressor idle from February 16 to April 11 while resistance heat carried the home, and the homeowner did not notice; auxiliary energy exceeded compressor energy.

Several prototype sites had long stretches (up to 3,444 hours) where the heat pump did not work as intended and the home ran on supplemental heat until manufacturer or contractor intervention; bills were not measured.

assertions.quote: THEY SAY THAT POWER KICKS IN WHEN TEMPERATURES DIP BELOW 40 TO 35
MANY TECHNICIANS ADVISE YOU TO NOT CHANGE THE THERMOSTAT IF YOU GO AWAY ON A SHORT VACATION OR EVEN AT NIGHT.

verdicts.note: Monitored UK heat pumps reach higher COPs with weather compensation and continuous low-temperature running, though setbacks can still save in leaky homes.
